analytic.title: Sensor Management in Real Time and a Camera Control Application for Air Vehicles

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Camera systems are increasingly utilized in Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR) missions on manned and unmanned aircraft. For manned missions, the automatic control of the camera field of view and orientation through pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) commands frees the pilot to perform higher cognitive functions. For unmanned missions, automatic PTZ commands enable higher degrees of autonomy. This paper addresses the problem of controlling the field of view and orientation of cameras mounted on air vehicles so that the resulting images of commanded areas of interest (AOIs) have specified ground sampling distances (GSDs). The problem is complicated by several factors: First, while the instantaneous positions of the vehicles are assumed to be known, their routes, including their altitude profiles, are not known in advance, which precludes preplanning. Second, the sizes of the AOIs are arbitrary, implying that a single look of the camera may not be sufficient to cover them. Third, the slew times of the cameras may be too slow, and the cameras may not operate while PTZ parameters are changing. Finally, given an AOI, the time intervals when the desired GSDs are achievable varies for different cameras. In the paper, we first show that successful collection of an AOI image (i.e. collection with a prescribed GSD) is only possible if the aircraft lies inside a spherical cap depending on the position of the AOI, and the desired GSD. Given a stream of requested AOIs, with corresponding GSDs and values characterizing their importance to a user, we then develop algorithms to service the most valuable ensemble of requests, while satisfying the requested GSDs. Three algorithms are developed: (1) a scheduling algorithm, for deciding which request to service at a given instant of time, (2) an admission control algorithm, enabling a graceful degradation in case of system overload (more requests than available timeline) and (3) an algorithm for deciding which of the platforms (air vehicle and camera) services a given request. We examine each of the three algorithms in turn. The scheduling algorithm is centered on the earliest deadline first (EDF) scheme from the real-time systems literature. Deadlines for servicing AOI requests are determined by computing the intersection between the extrapolated aircraft trajectory and the spherical caps defined earlier. The admission control algorithm is developed based on schedulability tests for EDF. Finally, the algorithm for routing the requests among platforms are based on machine shop scheduling problems, which essentially promote load balancing among the platforms. We introduce a heuristic called min-max utilization, inspired on the makespan minimization procedures developed for machine shop scheduling problems. Extensive simulation results are presented, illustrating the superior performance of the algorithms in contrast to other alternatives.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Attention to the discipline of sensor management has gained popularity in recent years, with the ever growing presence of sensor systems with diverse capabilities. From the academic side, sensor management leverages the disciplines of operations research, control theory, and real-time systems into procedures to optimize the usage of sensors [1]. From the industry side, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) problems arising in the defense industry have been the main source of interest [2], but more recently non-military applications have been reported [3]. This paper addresses the problem of controlling the fieldof-view and orientation of cameras mounted on air vehicles so that the resulting images of commanded Areas of Interest (AOIs) have specified ground sampling distances (GSDs). To solve this problem, we borrow and adapt fundamental results from the real-time systems literature [4]. Three types of algorithms are developed: (1) scheduling algorithms, for deciding which request to service at a given instant, (2) admission control algorithms, enabling a graceful degradation in case of system overload (more requests than available timeline) and (3) algorithms for deciding which of the platforms (air vehicle and camera) services a given request.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the problem of controlling the orientation of cameras mounted on air vehicles so that the resulting images of AOIs have specified GSDs. Section 3 presents related work and introduces a real-time systems computing model for describing the problem. Limitations of the model are discussed and relevant background material is presented. Section 4 presents an algorithm for controlling a single camera for viewing small AOIs. Here, small AOIs are those than can be covered with a single look of the camera. The algorithm combines a standard scheduling procedure with an admission control scheme, which is shown to improve performance under heavy loads. Section 5 extends the algorithms in Section 4 for controlling multiple cameras for viewing small AOIs. Specifically, in Section 5 we present an algorithm to decide which of the platforms will perform a given service request. Section 6 addresses the problem of controlling a single camera for viewing AOIs of arbitrary size. Section 7 closes the paper with our conclusions. Simulation results are presented throughout sections 4 to 6.

div.head: THE PROBLEM OF CAMERA CONTROL
div.p: We are given N ≥ 1 air vehicles, each with a mounted pantilt-zoom (PTZ) camera with n c angles of view φ k , k = 1, • • • , n c , and capable of producing images with n p ×n p pixels. Requests for viewing polygonal AOIs in the ground are continuously received by a command center, which decides which air vehicle to assign to each request, and compute PTZ camera commands for each request. Requests are given in terms of: (1) a desired GSD, representing the pixel resolution in the ground, (2) the position of the vertices of the polygon, and (3) a value for executing the request. The problem at hand is to service the most valuable ensemble of requests, while satisfying the desired GSDs. The problem is complicated by several factors:

1. The routes of the vehicles including their altitude profiles are not known. 2. The sizes of the AOIs are arbitrary, implying that a single look of the camera may not be sufficient to cover them. 3. The slew times of the cameras may be too slow, and the cameras may not operate while PTZ parameters are changing. 4. Given an AOI, the time intervals when the desired GSD are achievable vary for different cameras.

While we will relax a few of these factors while developing our algorithms, we notice that factor 4 above is of particular importance, introducing a class of problems not covered by available real-time systems computing models. We close this section with two propositions, relating the GSD with the kinematic parameters of the problem.

div.head: Operations research, control theory and real-time systems
div.p: Of the three disciplines usually invoked in the solution of sensor management problems -operations research, control theory, and real-time systems -it is the third one that is the most applicable to address the problem at hand. Indeed, operations research arises in planning problems for long time scales, when one knows the tasks a priori [5]. In the problem addressed in this paper, the tasks arrive in real time at very short time scales, and preplanning over a large horizon is not possible. Control theory is valuable when tasks are reactive, i.e. they induce a change in the state of the system, and Markov decision problems are naturally formulated [6], which is not the case in our problem. The real-time systems discipline is concerned with the proper scheduling of tasks to meet deadlines, and is discussed below.

div.head: Computing models for real-time systems
div.p: A large number of computing models exist to describe realtime processing in both one processor or more processors (see [7] for a recent survey). With increasing complexity one gains generality, and the ability to describe more intricate phenomena. However, one looses mathematical tractability.

The most basic and studied of these models is the Liu and Layland (L&L) model introduced in [8]. To keep the paper self-contained, we present the main highlights of the L&L model, and three propositions which form the basis of the algorithms studied on this paper.

The L&L model (see [4] for a detailed exposition) deals with a collection of tasks T i , i = 1, 2, • • • , n. Each task in the system has individual jobs J ij ,j = 1, 2, • • • . Each job J ij has an absolute deadline denoted by d ij . Hence, a job in T i that is released at time t must complete no later than D ij time units of time after t, where D ij = d ijt denotes the relative deadline of T i . The execution time e ij denotes the total amount of time needed to complete each job. The period p i of the task is the minimum length of all time intervals between release times of consecutive jobs in T i .

Remark 1: In our application, tasks have only one job. Therefore, we drop the second index j whenever it is clearly understood that job J i1 is the only job of task T i , with p i = ∞. On these cases, we also use the terms job and task interchangeably. Exceptions are clearly marked in the text.

By a schedule, we mean an assignment of all the jobs in the system on the available processors. In addition to these quantities in the L&L model, we also associate a value v i to each task. The value of the task quantifies the criticality of its execution to the user. We say that a schedule is feasible when every job completes by its deadline. We say that a set of jobs is schedulable by a given scheduling algorithm if the algorithm produces feasible schedules for the jobs. We say that a job is preemptable when its execution can be interrupted. A job is non-preemptable when its execution cannot be interrupted. While the bulk of the literature in real time systems is concerned with a large number or infinite jobs per task, and preemptable jobs, in our problem we are interested in situations where each task consists of a single, nonpreemtable job. The Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm prioritizes jobs according to their deadlines. The importance of EDF stems from Propositions 3 and 4 below.

Proposition 3: When preemption is allowed, the EDF algorithm can produce a feasible schedule for a set of jobs with arbitrary release times and deadlines on a processor if and only if there exists a feasible schedule for the set of jobs.
Proof: [4], page 81.

Proposition 4: When preemption is not allowed, the EDF algorithm can produce a feasible schedule for a set of jobs with arbitrary release times and deadlines on a processor if and only if there exists a feasible schedule which do not insert idle times for the set of jobs.
Proof: [9].

Propositions 3 and 4 recommend EDF scheduling for both the preemptive and non-preemptive cases. However, EDF perform poorly under overload, with tasks missing deadlines on an unpredictable way [10], [11]. To prevent overload, it is necessary to develop a schedulability test which characterizes the existence of a feasible schedule. Schedulability tests for EDF are readily available for the preemptive case. One way to develop a test for the non-preemptive case is to characterize the effect of non-preemption as a blocking of a task. In EDF scheduling, a job with an earlier deadline that becomes ready when a non-preemptive later deadline job is executing is blocked until the lower-priority job completes.
A schedulability test taking into account blocking times is presented in Proposition 5:
Proposition 5: A task T i with a total blocking time b i is schedulable with other periodic tasks on a processor according to the EDF algorithm if
div.formula: n i=1 e i min(D i , p i ) + b i min(D i , p i ) ≤ 1(3)
div.p: Proof: [4], page 178. In this case, tasks can have finite periods and multiple jobs. The following corollary examines the case where tasks have only one job.
Corollary 1: When tasks have only one job, a task/job is schedulable with other tasks/jobs according to the EDF algorithm if
div.formula: n i=1 e i D i + e i D i ≤ 1(4)
div.p: Proof: In the worst case, the blocking times of all tasks coincides with their execution times. Replacing b i with e i in equation (3), and assuming
div.formula: p i = ∞ for all i = 1, 2, • • • , n gives equation (4).
div.p: Corollary 1 gives a sufficient (not necessary) condition for EDF schedulability.

div.head: CONTROLLING ONE CAMERA FOR VIEWING SMALL AOIS
div.p: The algorithm

For each task/job, the release time and the deadline correspond to the instants of time when the air vehicle trajectory intersects the spherical cap described in Proposition 2. These instants of time can be estimated assuming the air vehicle follows a straight line with constant velocity. The critical events in our model are the termination of a task, and the release of a task. The algorithm has two components: task selection, triggered by the termination of a task, and admission control, triggered by the release of a task.
Motivated by Proposition 4 we utilize EDF as our scheduling discipline. Admission control is performed on basis of Corollary 1. Given n EDF-schedulable tasks, an n + 1-th task is accepted if:
div.formula: n i=1 e i D i + 2 e n+1 D n+1 ≤ 1(5)
div.p: In practice, we found the schedulability criterion defined by equation ( 5) to be too conservative. As an alternative, we utilize a small fudge factor δ to account for non-preemptability, and accept T n+1 if:
div.formula: n i=1 e i D i + e n+1 D n+1 ≤ 1 -δ (6)

div.head: Computer simulations
div.p: We compare the performance of the algorithm described above (called Aero2016-A) with two algorithms: the greedy distance (GD) algorithm where the closest AOI within the GSD circle is serviced; the EDF algorithm where the AOI with earliest deadline is serviced, without the schedulability test present in Aero2016-A. We consider a hypothetical scenario where the total area is a rectangle of 40 × 80 units of distance and small AOIs are randomly generated inside the rectangle. The air vehicle flies at constant velocity, along a straight line route perpendicular to the rectangle, as

shown in Figure 3. The air vehicle flies at constant altitude of 6 units of distance. In this case, the GSD condition is equivalent to having the projection of the air vehicle in the ground to be a circle with radius given by equation ( 1). The circle is the intersection of the spherical cap in Figure 2 with the ground plane. Two parameters are varied in our experiments: the total number of randomly generated AOIs (50/100/150/200) and the slew time τ of the camera (3/5/7 units of time). Increasing both parameters (individually or jointly) stresses the operation of the system, i.e. one should expect degradation in performance in both cases. The results are presented on Table The results can be summarized as follows:
• The Aero2016-A algorithm is the best overall, providing competitive scores with light loads and heavy loads.

• EDF collapses for heavy loads, a phenomenon well known in the literature [10], [11]. The reason is that under high loads, the job with earliest deadline is the most likely to miss the deadline causing other jobs with larger deadlines to miss their deadlines as well. This cascade effect is alleviated by the admission control procedure in Aero2016-A, as illustrated in Remark 3.

• On a first approximation, the GD scheme is essentially a random scheme, due to the lack of correlation between the distance and the geometry determining the region of desired GSDs. For very heavy loads, even Aero2016-A is inferior to GD, resulting from the algorithm's residual reliance on earliest deadlines for scheduling.

Remark 3: To illustrate how admission control alleviates the cascade effect faced by EDF scheduling under heavy loads, we consider the following example involving five jobs with parameters given in Table 2. Remark 4: To take into account the priorities of the AOIs, one can modify the admission control test so that high priority requests (those with higher v i ) can replace low priority requests in the queue, waiting for service.

div.head: CONTROLLING MULTIPLE CAMERAS FOR VIEWING SMALL AOIS
div.p: The algorithm Current multiprocessor scheduling models [7] assume that tasks/jobs have identical deadlines in each processor. In our problem, given the GSD d , the deadlines for each camera are the instants of time we predict the air vehicle exits the spherical cap (Figure 2). These are different for each air vehicle, a situation that is not allowed for current models.

When deadlines are not a concern, the problem of assigning jobs to processors can be casted into the problem of makespan minimization. The problem is a follows: one has a number of jobs, and a number P of identical processors. We define the makespan of an assignment (or schedule) as the time it takes for the schedule to complete, that is when all jobs have completed processing. We are interested in the online makespan minimization problem, where jobs are assigned to processors as they arrive and must be processed without interruption. Graham's List algorithm - [12], [13] proceeds by assigning jobs to the processor which has received the least amount of service until that time. The List algorithm is optimal when the number of processors is 2 or 3, since it produces the minimal possible makespan in these cases [14].
It is clear that the List algorithm performs load balancing between the processors.
Inspired by the List algorithm, and taking into account the job deadlines, we introduce the min-max utilization heuristic as follows.

1. Assume the execution times of the requests to be the same in each processor, but the deadlines to be different. 2. div.head: Computer simulations
div.p: We compare the performance of the min-max utilization heuristic (called Aero2016-B here) with Graham's List algorithm, centered in load balance. The air vehicles travel along parallel straight lines, 9.25 units of distance apart. We follow the same simulation setup as in Figure 3 with one difference.

Here, instead of having the AOIs laid down at the start of the experiment, we divide the AOIs into two classes: half of the AOIs are laid down a priori, while the other half "pop-up" at various stages in the simulation. This allows AOIs to appear in the fields of view of the two platforms simultaneously, therefore exercising the Aero2016-B algorithm. The results in Table 3 show that Aero2016-B consistently outperform the List algorithm for the metric of completed requests. We recall that List was not designed with deadlines in mind. So, its optimality for makespan minimization is not in question here.

div.head: CONTROLLING ONE CAMERA FOR VIEWING LARGE AOIS
div.p: The algorithm When an AOI does not fit into the footprint of a single camera look, it is necessary to tessellate the AOI with smaller tiles, each corresponding to a single camera look. This process gives rise to a substantially more complex problem, where the jobs now correspond to individual tiles. For slow air vehicle speeds, the tessellation process needs to occur just once, whenever the air vehicle enters the spherical cap corresponding to the AOI. For faster speeds, however, the tiles may become stale as shown in Figure 4. The AOI marked in blue is first tessellated as shown in the left panel. As shown in the right panel, four tiles (marked in green) are serviced while the air vehicle moves East. However, continuing to service tiles according to the original tessellation is clearly not acceptable. Retessellation of the region given by the difference between the original AOI and the four tiles in green is then performed. The algorithm, called Aero2016-C, handles the creation and destruction of jobs associated with each tile, but preserves a link between the tiles and the original AOIs. For any tile, Aero2016-C is aware of how much of the AOI has been already covered and can estimate how many additional looks are needed, based on the average area of past camera views. At any instant, the tile to be serviced is the one for which the smallest positive slack time is available to complete the whole AOI. Aero2016-C does not tile AOIs with negative slack times, i.e. tiles for which there is no time remaining to complete the corresponding AOI.

div.head: Computer simulations
div.p: Table 4 presents the results, comparing Aero2016-C with greedy distance (GD) and EDF. For reference, depending on their size, AOIs are tessellated into 5 to 20 tiles. For light to moderate loads, ACC2016-C outperforms the other two schemes. For higher loads however, GD is preferred. This phenomenon is similar to the one observed in the case of small AOIs (Section 4) and explained by the residual dependence of Aero2016-C on deadlines, in contrast to the essentially random operation of GD.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper examined the problem of controlling the field of view and orientation of PTZ cameras so that the resulting images of commanded AOIs have a desired GSD. Approaches relying on real-time systems theory were proposed, and were shown to outperform other alternatives. Below, we present a number of further areas for research motivated by this work.

• Decentralized sensor management: The algorithm Aero2016-B (min-max heuristic) assumes the existence of a processing center -which can be located in one of the air vehicles -having complete information about the state of both platforms. Such a centralized scheme relies on stable communication links between the air vehicles, which may not be the case in many scenarios. In a decentralized scheme, a communication protocol is established allowing the platforms to exchange the information needed for decision making. The design of a such a protocol, and the exact nature of the decentralized decision problem under possible link instability represent an area of relevant, further research.

• Controlling multiple cameras for viewing large AOIs: This is a more complex problem than the ones tackled in this paper, even assuming a centralized setup. The reason is that the platforms have distinct fields of view with respect to the AOI, and therefore the tessellation solutions would be different: a tile produced by a tessellation done by one platform may not coverable by the other platform. Suboptimal heuristics certainly exist, such as assigning entire AOIs to a single platform, and solving the problem as in Section 6. However, it is not clear how effective such heuristics can be when compared to a truly collaborative solution combining both platforms.
